strengths: The paper addresses an important bottleneck for indoor semantic occupancy: acquiring scalable 3D supervision. Leveraging in-the-wild house-tour videos and modern 3D reconstruction/VFM tools is a timely and potentially impactful direction for computer vision.

The proposed pipeline is conceptually useful: video curation, indoor filtering, Dust3R-based camera/depth recovery, semantic pseudo-labeling, voxelization, and region-level 2D-to-3D distillation form a plausible recipe for learning occupancy representations without calibrated capture hardware.

The experiments cover two relevant indoor occupancy benchmarks, NYUv2 and OccScanNet, and include full-label, low-label, cross-dataset pretraining, and zero-shot evaluations. The NYUv2 low-label results are particularly promising, e.g. sizable mIoU gains at 10% and 20% labels.
The method is mostly architecture-light and uses Symphonies as a backbone, which makes the pretraining idea potentially reusable with other occupancy networks.

The paper includes implementation details such as optimizer, learning rates, schedule, batch size, GPUs, and dataset splits, and acknowledges some limitations, including non-release of YouTube-Occ and unmodeled dynamic/static distinctions.
weaknesses: The main scientific claims are overstated relative to the evidence. The abstract claims state-of-the-art zero-shot performance, but the zero-shot table reports very low performance on NYUv2 and OccScanNet and provides no zero-shot baseline comparison. This is a consequential mismatch between claim and evidence.

The practical contribution is weakened because YouTube-Occ will not be publicly released. Since the dataset/pipeline is central to the paper, lack of data release substantially limits reproducibility, verification of curation quality, and community impact. The paper also gives limited detail on YouTube licensing/terms, consent/privacy, and whether house-tour data may include sensitive interiors.

The reported improvements over the strong Symphonies baseline are often small: +1.04 mIoU on NYUv2 full labels and only +0.30 mIoU on OccScanNet full labels, with no error bars or repeated runs. On OccScanNet low-label settings, gains are marginal and sometimes IoU decreases, so it is hard to know whether improvements are statistically meaningful.

There are insufficient ablations to isolate what matters. The paper does not convincingly separate the effects of YouTube-Occ data, Dust3R reconstruction quality, SAN masks, DINOv2 features, superpixel/supervoxel pooling, contrastive loss, and pseudo-semantic voxel supervision. Comparisons to simpler pretraining alternatives or image-level distillation baselines are missing.

The quality and accuracy of the automatically reconstructed occupancy labels are not adequately evaluated. The pipeline relies on heuristic scaling by assumed wall height, z-up alignment, outlier filtering, and pseudo-label semantic segmentation, but there is no quantitative audit of reconstruction errors, scale errors, semantic noise, or how these propagate to occupancy learning.

Some result discussion appears incorrect or misleading. For example, the OccScanNet text claims large improvements for television, object, and furniture, but the table shows only very small gains over Symphonies for those classes. Such inconsistencies reduce confidence in the experimental analysis.

The paper is better characterized as an Applied/Systems or Dataset/Benchmark contribution than a purely Algorithms/General paper, because the main novelty is the Internet-video data pipeline and pretraining setup. Under that framing, the lack of released data, limited documentation, and limited validation of the constructed dataset are more serious weaknesses.

The presentation has several clarity and polish issues, including section-numbering inconsistencies, grammatical errors, vague descriptions of clip splitting/filtering, and limited detail on how pseudo-label classes are mapped to the 13 occupancy classes. These do not invalidate the work, but they make reproduction and assessment harder.

strengths: The paper targets an important problem: reducing dependence on expensive indoor 3D semantic occupancy annotations and acquisition setups by leveraging internet videos and 2D foundation models.

The proposed YouTube-Occ pipeline is conceptually interesting. Using house-tour videos, Dust3R-based camera/depth reconstruction, VFM semantic labeling, voxelization, and region-level 2D-to-3D distillation is a plausible direction for scalable indoor 3D pretraining.
The method is simple and model-agnostic in principle, requiring only pretraining of the occupancy backbone and leaving the downstream occupancy head to be fine-tuned normally.

The paper includes evaluations on NYUv2 and OccScanNet, annotation-efficiency experiments, cross-dataset pretraining, zero-shot evaluation, and some ablations through varying label budgets, which are relevant to the central claims.
weaknesses: The empirical gains are too small to support the strong claims of state-of-the-art performance. On NYUv2 the improvement over Symphonies is only +1.04 mIoU and +1.21 IoU, and on OccScanNet it is only +0.30 mIoU and +0.25 IoU. These margins are not accompanied by multiple runs, error bars, or significance tests, so they may be within ordinary training variance.

The most important claimed contribution, learning from YouTube-Occ, is weakly supported. Cross-dataset pretraining gives modest gains on NYUv2 but only tiny gains on OccScanNet: for example +0.06 mIoU at 10%, +0.34 at 20%, +0.27 at 50%, and even a lower IoU at 50%. This does not convincingly demonstrate a powerful internet-data pretraining signal.

The zero-shot results are very poor: 9.95 mIoU on NYUv2 and 4.61 mIoU on OccScanNet. The paper presents this as a possible future direction, but it undercuts the abstract/introduction claim that spatially accurate training can be achieved from internet data without camera pre-knowledge.

The dataset contribution is substantially weakened because YouTube-Occ will not be publicly released. Since the dataset and automated pipeline are central to the paper, non-release makes the work difficult to verify, reproduce, or build upon, especially given the many heuristic processing steps.

Key dataset-quality issues are not adequately validated. The pipeline relies on Dust3R reconstructions, heuristic outlier filtering, assumed 2.8m wall height scaling, z-up alignment, semantic labels from SAN, and voxel majority voting, but the paper provides little quantitative assessment of reconstruction accuracy, scale accuracy, semantic label noise, or occupancy label quality.

The novelty is limited. The method combines existing components: 2D foundation features, segmentation masks/superpixels, 2D-3D feature alignment, contrastive distillation, and reconstruction from monocular video. The paper does not provide a sufficiently distinctive algorithmic insight beyond this combination.

Some experimental claims are overstated or internally misleading. For OccScanNet, the text claims substantial improvements for categories such as television, object, and furniture, but relative to the strongest baseline Symphonies these improvements are small; the large numbers appear to compare against weaker methods rather than the actual prior state of the art.

The comparison set is not fully convincing for a pretraining/data paper. The work should compare against stronger or more direct alternatives such as DINO feature distillation without superpixels, pixel-level or image-level distillation, pretraining on NYUv2/ScanNet RGB-D-style data, Dust3R-derived geometry without semantic distillation, and other recent self-supervised 3D representation methods under matched settings.

Protocol details remain ambiguous. It is not always clear whether pretraining is done on the same target training images before supervised fine-tuning, on YouTube-Occ, or both; how validation data and hyperparameters are selected; and how label-budget subsets are sampled. This ambiguity matters because the reported gains are small.

The societal and licensing discussion is inadequate for scraped YouTube videos of private indoor homes. The paper does not clearly address consent, YouTube terms, privacy filtering, copyright/licensing of videos, or risks from reconstructing private interiors, despite using these videos as a central data source.

The writing and presentation have several clarity problems, including grammatical errors, inconsistent naming of YouTube-Occ/YouTube-OCC, a mistaken section reference, and imprecise descriptions of the method. These do not alone determine the score, but they add to the reproducibility concerns.

strengths: The paper tackles an important bottleneck for indoor 3D semantic occupancy: lack of scalable annotated data. Using YouTube real-estate videos with automatic reconstruction, semantic labeling, and voxelization is a timely and practically meaningful direction for the community.

The technical idea of region-level 2D-to-3D distillation is well motivated. Superpixel/supervoxel alignment using SAN masks and DINOv2 features is a sensible way to transfer semantic priors while avoiding noisy pixel-level correspondences in cluttered indoor scenes.

The empirical results are consistently positive on NYUv2 and OccScanNet. The strongest evidence is in annotation-efficient fine-tuning, especially on NYUv2 where gains are substantial under 10% and 20% labeled data, supporting the claim that pretraining improves representation quality.
The paper studies both benchmark pretraining and cross-dataset YouTube-Occ pretraining, which helps separate the value of the self-supervised objective from the value of Internet-scale indoor data.
The work is clearly relevant to ECCV: it combines 3D reconstruction, vision foundation models, web-data learning, and indoor semantic occupancy prediction in a coherent system.
weaknesses: The YouTube-Occ dataset is central to the paper but will not be publicly released. This significantly limits reproducibility, independent verification of data quality, and downstream impact as a data contribution. It also makes the contribution closer to an algorithm/systems paper than a reusable benchmark/dataset paper.

Several important pipeline choices are heuristic and insufficiently validated: Dust3R reconstruction quality, outlier filtering, z-up alignment, wall-height-based metric scaling, semantic labeling noise, and voxelization errors. Since the method depends on pseudo-3D supervision from Internet videos, stronger quantitative quality analysis would make the scientific case more convincing.

The gains over the strongest baseline are modest in the fully supervised setting, especially on OccScanNet (+0.30 mIoU, +0.25 IoU). The paper sometimes describes these as substantial, but the actual margins are small and no statistical significance or multiple-run variance is reported.

Ablations are limited. The paper would benefit from isolating the effects of superpixel grouping versus pixel/global distillation, DINOv2 versus other embeddings, SAN mask quality, dataset size, YouTube-Occ versus standard in-domain unlabeled pretraining, and each reconstruction/filtering step.

There are some accuracy and clarity issues in the result discussion. For example, the OccScanNet text claims large improvements for television, object, and furniture, but Table 2 shows only tiny gains over Symphonies for those classes; the large numbers appear to compare against weaker baselines rather than the main baseline.

The zero-shot results from YouTube-Occ to NYUv2 and OccScanNet are quite low, which suggests a sizable domain and pseudo-label gap. The paper acknowledges this only briefly and could better characterize when web-video pretraining is expected to help.

Ethical and legal handling of YouTube data is underdeveloped. The paper cites privacy concerns and says the dataset will not be released, but it does not sufficiently discuss video terms of use, consent, copyright/licensing, or safeguards for scraped indoor home footage.

strengths: The paper addresses an important bottleneck for indoor 3D semantic occupancy: the scarcity and privacy burden of annotated RGB-D/3D data. Using uncalibrated internet videos as pre-training data is a timely and potentially impactful direction for computer vision.

The proposed YouTube-Occ pipeline is reasonably complete: video filtering, camera/point-cloud reconstruction with Dust3R, semantic pseudo-labeling with open-vocabulary segmentation, voxelization, and downstream pre-training. This makes the contribution more than a single architectural tweak.

The pre-training method is model-agnostic and is evaluated on multiple occupancy architectures. The reported gains are consistent across Symphonies, EmbodiedOcc, and MonoScene, with especially meaningful improvements in few-shot settings.

The experiments include useful diagnostics: the authors show that naive pseudo-label supervision transfers poorly, compare against several auxiliary/pre-training strategies, and ablate both the region and prototype alignment losses as well as projection/prototype design choices.
The paper is generally clearly written, with a coherent motivation and a good explanation of why direct supervision from noisy web pseudo-labels is insufficient.
weaknesses: The core empirical gains under full supervision are modest: for example, Symphonies improves by about +1.95 mIoU on NYUv2 and +1.67 mIoU on Occ-ScanNet. These are useful but not overwhelmingly strong given the extra web-data pipeline, foundation models, and pre-training stage.

The quality, composition, and reproducibility of YouTube-Occ are under-specified. The paper gives counts of frames/scenes but little detail on video selection criteria, channel diversity, deduplication, train/test leakage risk with benchmark-like real-estate scenes, failure rates of reconstruction/filtering, or whether the YouTube data can actually be redistributed under license constraints.

The reconstruction and scale normalization pipeline relies on brittle heuristics, especially the 2.8-meter wall-height assumption and z-up/floor alignment. The paper acknowledges this limitation but does not quantify sensitivity to scale errors or reconstruction failures, even though these are central to using uncalibrated web videos.

Comparisons are somewhat limited. The paper compares plug-in losses and Pri3D, but does not convincingly adapt or compare against stronger recent self-supervised occupancy methods in the indoor setting, nor does it isolate how much benefit comes from DINOv2/SAN distillation versus the YouTube video data itself.

The evaluation is restricted to two indoor benchmarks with similar semantic taxonomies and voxel settings. Claims about generalizable web-scale 3D priors would be stronger with cross-dataset/domain evaluations beyond NYUv2 and Occ-ScanNet, or with tests on more diverse indoor layouts and camera styles.

The pseudo-labels themselves appear weak when used directly, and Table 1 shows negative transfer for naive joint training. The proposed pre-training overcomes this to some extent, but the paper does not deeply analyze which pseudo-label errors matter, which scene types fail, or how often the automated pipeline produces unusable labels.

Some implementation details needed for reproduction are missing or too high-level, including exact prompt/class mappings for SAN, filtering thresholds, Dust3R post-processing heuristics, voxel bounding-box definition, prototype initialization/update details, and compute/storage cost for building YouTube-Occ.

strengths: The paper tackles an important bottleneck for indoor 3D semantic occupancy: limited annotated 3D data. Using uncalibrated web videos as a scalable pretraining source is a relevant and potentially impactful direction for computer vision.

The proposed pipeline is practically motivated and combines recent 3D/2D foundation models, including Dust3R-style reconstruction, open-vocabulary segmentation, DINOv2 feature distillation, voxel-anchored Gaussian rendering, and prototype contrastive alignment into an end-to-end pretraining recipe.

The experiments show consistent positive gains over reproduced baselines across several architectures and two benchmarks. The few-shot results are the most convincing part: YouTube-Occ pretraining improves Symphonies by about 3-5 mIoU on NYUv2 at 5-10% labels and about 1.7-2.4 mIoU on Occ-ScanNet at 5-10% labels.
The ablations are useful: both the region loss and prototype loss contribute, and the projection/prototype design choices are tested rather than simply asserted.
weaknesses: The central evidence for the web-data pipeline is not fully convincing. The generated pseudo-labels themselves are very weak on Occ-ScanNet, and direct zero-shot or joint training performs poorly or even hurts mIoU. The paper then shifts to a distillation/pretraining framework, but it remains unclear how much of the gain comes from YouTube-scale web data versus generic DINOv2/SAN feature distillation and in-domain training effects.

The performance improvements under full supervision are modest: roughly +1-2 mIoU for the strongest setting, and only +0.76 mIoU from YouTube-Occ on full Occ-ScanNet in Table 3. These gains may be useful, but they are not strong enough to fully support the broad claims about extracting rich 3D priors from in-the-wild videos without more analysis.

The comparison is incomplete for the claimed contribution. The paper says prior self-supervised occupancy approaches cannot transfer to uncalibrated indoor web videos, but it does not adapt or compare against stronger relevant self-supervised/distillation baselines under the same data and architecture budget. Table 4 is narrow and only on NYUv2, with limited explanation of fairness and tuning.

The dataset and pipeline description lacks important reproducibility details: exact video selection protocol, channel/query list, filtering thresholds, clip statistics, failure rates, reconstruction-quality filtering, wall-height normalization details, camera/scale validation, class-mapping rules, and train/validation leakage controls are underspecified. Since the contribution is partly data-centric, these omissions are consequential.

The use of YouTube real-estate videos raises licensing, privacy, and release concerns, but the manuscript only says the data/code will be released and does not discuss whether redistribution is permitted, whether faces/personal information appear, or how takedowns/copyright are handled.

The method is somewhat incremental technically: most heavy lifting comes from existing foundation models and known feature-distillation/contrastive/prototype mechanisms. Voxel-anchored Gaussianization is reasonable, but the paper does not sufficiently isolate it from simpler projection or distillation baselines across datasets and architectures.

Some experimental interpretations are overstated. For example, in-domain pretraining rows in Table 3 appear stronger than YouTube-Occ in several cases, which weakens the claim that web videos provide uniquely robust generalizable representations. The paper should discuss this more directly.

Clarity is uneven. The pseudo-label evaluation in Table 1 is confusing, the text appears to refer to an NYUv2 joint-training baseline while the table lists NYUv2 + Occ-ScanNet, and several implementation choices are described at a high level rather than precisely enough for replication.

strengths: The paper tackles an important bottleneck in indoor 3D semantic occupancy: scarcity of large annotated 3D indoor data. Using uncalibrated in-the-wild videos as pre-training data is a timely and practically significant direction.

The proposed YouTube-Occ pipeline is compelling as a systems/data contribution: it combines video filtering, Dust3R-based reconstruction, open-vocabulary 2D segmentation, voxelization, and pseudo-label generation into an automated source of 100k+ frames across 5k+ scenes.

The paper does not merely assume pseudo-labels are sufficient; it identifies that naive supervised use of the pseudo-labels gives poor or negative transfer, then proposes a more appropriate feature-distillation pre-training framework.

The dual alignment design is technically reasonable: voxel-anchored Gaussianization aligns 3D voxel features to 2D teacher features within a frame, while prototype contrastive learning encourages cross-scene semantic consistency.

Experimental evidence is broad for the problem setting. Gains are shown on NYUv2 and Occ-ScanNet, across three different occupancy architectures, and especially in limited-label settings where the benefits are most meaningful.
Ablations support the contribution: both region and prototype losses help, and the Gaussianization/prototype choices are compared against plausible variants.
The paper is generally clear and well structured, with a strong motivation, readable method presentation, and useful qualitative visualizations.
weaknesses: The full-data improvements, while consistent, are relatively modest: for the strongest Symphonies baseline, gains are about +1.95 mIoU on NYUv2 and +1.67 mIoU on Occ-ScanNet. The main impact is more convincing in few-shot settings than as a general SOTA improvement.

The contribution type is not explicitly declared. I would assess it closer to an Applied/Systems and data-centric contribution than a purely algorithmic one; under that lens it is strong, but the paper should provide more dataset/pipeline documentation to fully support the claimed scalability and reproducibility.

Reproducibility of the YouTube data pipeline is under-specified. Details such as video source selection, filtering thresholds, clip sampling, reconstruction failure rates, scale normalization failures, and expected compute/storage costs are not sufficiently quantified.

The pipeline depends heavily on foundation models and heuristic assumptions, especially Dust3R reconstruction, SAN segmentation, and the fixed 2.8 m wall-height metric-scale prior. The paper acknowledges some limitations but does not deeply analyze failure modes or sensitivity to these assumptions.

The evaluation is limited to two indoor benchmarks with the same broad 11 semantic classes and mostly single-frame occupancy architectures. It remains unclear how well the learned priors transfer to more diverse indoor taxonomies, active robotics settings, multi-view/temporal models, or non-real-estate internet videos.

Comparisons to recent self-supervised or pseudo-label-based occupancy methods are somewhat indirect. The paper argues that outdoor methods are not directly applicable, which is plausible, but more adapted baselines or stronger alternative pre-training recipes would make the empirical case firmer.

The societal and data governance aspects of using YouTube/real-estate videos are not sufficiently discussed. Even if the videos are publicly available, copyright, consent, privacy leakage, and redistribution constraints matter for a dataset-style contribution.
